sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
October 2026 delivered a sharply bifurcated global equity tape, defined by a violent divergence between AI-driven mega-cap technology and the broader market. The S&P 500 declined **0.9%** to close at **7,580**, the Nasdaq Composite shed **5.3%** to **25,437** — its worst monthly performance since March 2025 — and the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced **1.7%** to **51,770**. The month's most striking structural signal was the equal-weight S&P 500's estimated **5%** gain, representing the widest divergence in favour of the average company versus the cap-weighted index since 2009.

Across international markets the picture was broadly negative outside of select European benchmarks. The Shanghai Composite fell **6.3%** to close at **3,599** — widely characterised as the index's worst monthly performance in nearly a decade — while the Hang Seng declined approximately **5.4%** (approx., verify before merging) and the Nikkei 225 fell an estimated **4%–5%** (approx., verify before merging). European bourses proved more resilient: the FTSE 100 gained approximately **1.2%** (approx., verify before merging) and the DAX registered a mixed result that varied across sources (approx., verify before merging). The common thread across underperforming markets was concentrated exposure to AI-related valuations, elevated energy import costs, and the global repricing of risk against a backdrop of US 10-year yields threatening **5%**.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
AI Megacap De-Risking Triggers Worst Nasdaq Month Since March 2025 -- The Nasdaq Composite's **5.3%** October decline — its worst monthly performance since March 2025 — was driven by a sharp reassessment of AI-related valuations as investor focus shifted from capital expenditure announcements to earnings conversion timelines. Technology and AI infrastructure names that commanded premium multiples throughout 2026 faced aggressive multiple compression as the market demanded near-term free cash flow evidence rather than long-horizon narratives, and de-risking from crowded positions cascaded across the sector.

The rotation dynamic was striking in its breadth: the equal-weight S&P 500 gained an estimated **5%** for October, the widest gap in favour of the average company versus the cap-weighted index since 2009, as capital migrated into value, industrials, and energy. The Dow's concurrent **1.7%** advance to **51,770** underscored the same narrative — industrial, financial, and energy names absorbed flows departing the technology complex. Internationally, the Shanghai Composite's **6.3%** decline and the Hang Seng's approximate **5.4%** (approx., verify before merging) loss were also partly attributable to AI valuation reassessment, confirming the de-risking as a global rather than US-idiosyncratic adjustment.

Fed Holds at 3.75%–4.00% with Hawkish Dissents, December Hike Firmly in Play -- The FOMC's October 28 decision to hold the federal funds target at **3.75%–4.00%** was accompanied by a 10-2 vote, with two governors dissenting in favour of an immediate **25 basis point** hike — the first internal split in this tightening cycle. Chair Warsh's subsequent communications made clear the hold was tactical rather than a pivot signal, keeping December's meeting squarely in play for an additional move. Market participants repriced December hike probabilities materially higher through the month, and several major sell-side firms publicly projected further tightening extending into Q1 2027.

The persistence of above-target inflation — amplified by the energy price shock from Middle East supply disruptions — underpinned the hawkish minority's position. Bond markets initially sold off on the split decision, with the 10-year yield reaching an intraday high of **5.36%** — its highest level since 2002 — before risk-off flows from the equity sell-off generated a flight-to-quality bid that pulled yields back toward **4.96%** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end. The evolving Fed narrative — pause with intent — represents the central macro uncertainty heading into the Q4 close, with the December FOMC meeting widely expected to deliver the next rate move.

Middle East Energy Shock Sustains Crude Surge and Complicates Inflation Outlook -- Escalating attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz kept crude prices at elevated levels through October, with Brent trading in the **$107–$113/bbl** range (approx., verify before merging) and WTI settling around **$103–$104/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end. The energy complex extended its year-to-date advance to approximately **58%** (approx., verify before merging), as the geopolitical risk premium widened materially on the probability of sustained disruption to one of the world's most critical oil transit chokepoints. US energy equities surged approximately **13%** in October, acting as the primary counterweight to technology's collapse and the most important driver of the Dow's outperformance relative to the Nasdaq.

The energy shock presented a structural complication for central banks globally: persistently elevated crude prices feed directly into CPI and PCE readings, constraining rate-cutting optionality even as growth data moderated in some regions. For the Fed, the energy-driven inflation component reinforced the case made by the two hawkish dissenters and contributed to market repricing of December hike probabilities. For energy-importing APAC economies, the crude price surge added to current account deterioration and further complicated domestic monetary policy decisions, reinforcing the structural divergence between resource-exporting and resource-importing equity markets that has characterised 2026.

Treasury Yield Spike to 5.36% Reprices Global Risk Assets -- The 10-year US Treasury yield's intraday surge to **5.36%** — its highest level since 2002 — was October's most consequential fixed-income development, repricing discount rates across equities, credit, and real assets simultaneously. The move was catalyzed by a confluence of hotter-than-expected US inflation data, the energy price shock, and the FOMC's split vote signalling ongoing tightening risk. The global rate contagion was visible across European and APAC bond markets, with yields broadly higher even in economies where central banks had recently paused.

The subsequent partial Treasury rally — with the 10-year retreating toward **4.96%** (approx., verify before merging) by late October — was driven by risk-off safe-haven flows as the AI-driven equity sell-off generated flight-to-quality demand powerful enough to temporarily override the inflationary backdrop. The 2-year yield settled near **4.63%** (approx., verify before merging), leaving the 10-year/2-year spread at approximately **+33 basis points** (approx., verify before merging). For equity markets, the prolonged period of yields threatening **5%** proved particularly destabilising for long-duration growth assets, directly amplifying the Nasdaq's tech selloff, while simultaneously supporting financial sector earnings through wider net interest margins.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
The defining narrative in US equities was the violent unwinding of crowded AI and technology positions, with the Nasdaq's **5.3%** decline to **25,437** standing in sharp contrast to cyclical and value-oriented sectors. AI infrastructure stocks that had led the year's rally faced renewed scrutiny as investors pivoted from evaluating spending commitments to demanding tangible earnings conversion, triggering outsized multiple compression in megacap technology names. The convergence of this de-rating and the concurrent energy price surge produced an unusual tape in which the Dow gained **1.7%** to **51,770** in the same month that the Nasdaq posted its worst monthly loss since March 2025.

The Fed's October 28 decision to hold at **3.75%–4.00%** with two hawkish dissents reinforced the view that the tightening cycle is not definitively over, adding to multiple-compression pressure on long-duration growth assets and further weighing on rate-sensitive technology valuations. The equal-weight S&P 500's estimated **5%** monthly advance — the widest divergence in favour of the average company versus the cap-weighted index since 2009 — confirmed that breadth improved significantly even as the headline index posted a marginal **0.9%** decline to **7,580**. October raised a structural question that will define Q4 earnings season: how long can institutional investors sustain technology multiples embedding multi-year AI payback assumptions when the Fed has signalled further tightening and 10-year yields tested **5.36%**?

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities proved relatively resilient against the global risk-off backdrop, with the energy-heavy FTSE 100 gaining approximately **1.2%** (approx., verify before merging) as integrated energy names acted as powerful index tailwinds amid crude's sustained elevation — a performance characterised by some market commentators as the index's first monthly gain in three. The CAC 40 finished essentially flat, its diversified composition between luxury goods, financials, and energy partially offsetting technology-sector de-rating pressure. The DAX's outcome was less clear-cut, with available sources providing conflicting readings (approx., verify before merging) that likely reflect its greater exposure to technology hardware, automotive, and industrial cyclicals facing both the AI earnings shock and continued Chinese end-market demand softness.

European central bank policy trajectories remained in focus through October. Currency dynamics — with EUR/USD settling near **1.1206** — provided a modest tailwind for European export earnings, while energy sector constituents received meaningful support from elevated crude prices. The November macro outlook is complicated by oil above **$100/bbl** reigniting consumer energy inflation across the eurozone and UK, with the ECB facing conflicting signals between resurgent energy prices and below-trend domestic demand — particularly in Germany, where export sensitivity to a subdued Chinese growth environment continues to weigh on the region's most important industrial economy.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian equity markets bore disproportionate October losses, with the Shanghai Composite's **6.3%** decline to **3,599** representing one of the most severe monthly performances for the mainland index in nearly a decade. The sell-off reflected a convergence of domestic and international headwinds: a global reassessment of AI hardware valuations, subdued Chinese domestic demand, and the PBOC's decision to hold the Loan Prime Rate steady — disappointing markets that had anticipated targeted stimulus. Persistent foreign capital outflows amplified by risk-off global sentiment compounded the pressure on mainland equities.

The Hang Seng fell approximately **5.4%** (approx., verify before merging) as Hong Kong-listed technology names faced combined headwinds of global risk-off sentiment, elevated oil import costs, and capital outflows. The Nikkei 225 declined an estimated **4%–5%** (approx., verify before merging) as yen weakness — with USD/JPY near **157.56** — complicated the Bank of Japan's policy calculus around intervention thresholds even as it provided a marginal tailwind for exporters. Post-month, Chinese authorities signalled fresh market support measures, underscoring official concern about equity market stability ahead of year-end, though the structural headwinds from tightening global financial conditions and energy import costs remain formidable.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar navigated a complex backdrop in October, with the DXY consolidating near **101.75** (approx., verify before merging) as competing macro forces kept the greenback range-bound despite the volatile backdrop. The Fed's hawkish hold with two explicit dissents argued for dollar strength; the AI-driven equity sell-off and flight-to-quality Treasury demand created ambiguous risk sentiment that limited DXY upside, producing one of the more directionally uncertain months for the greenback in the current cycle.

Dollar performance diverged sharply across individual pairs. USD/JPY held elevated near **157.56**, reflecting the persistent gap between Fed and Bank of Japan policy trajectories — with yen levels well above thresholds that have historically prompted intervention discussion, though no intervention materialized. EUR/USD settled near **1.1206** as European macro data remained marginally constructive, while GBP/USD closed near **1.3397**, with sterling proving the relative FX outperformer as UK data continued to support a relatively hawkish Bank of England stance. Emerging market currencies broadly faced pressure from the combination of US yields threatening **5%** and rising energy import costs, adding to external balance sheet stress across current account deficit economies heading into year-end.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy markets dominated October's commodity narrative as the geopolitical risk premium from Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions kept crude prices elevated through the month. Brent traded in the **$107–$113/bbl** range (approx., verify before merging) and WTI settled around **$103–$104/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end, with the energy complex extending its year-to-date advance to approximately **58%** (approx., verify before merging). US energy equities surged approximately **13%** in October, acting as the primary counterweight to technology's collapse and the single most important driver of the Dow's outperformance relative to the Nasdaq for the month.

Gold registered a sharp reversal, falling approximately **6.3%** to close near **$3,913/oz** — a significant retracement from earlier 2026 highs — as rising real yields weighed on the non-yielding metal and the initial safe-haven impulse faded once the Fed held rather than pivoting dovishly. The Fed's hawkish hold with two dissents and oil-driven inflation expectations reinforced a higher-for-longer rate narrative that erodes the investment case for bullion, while significant ETF outflows accelerated the decline. Copper on COMEX settled near **$6.50/lb** (approx., verify before merging), reflecting constructive global infrastructure spending demand despite the softer Chinese growth backdrop — though base metals' relative stability amid broader commodity volatility underscored the selective, geopolitically-driven nature of October's energy surge rather than a demand-side commodity cycle.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
October was a month of elevated volatility in the US rates complex, with the 10-year Treasury yield reaching an intraday high of **5.36%** — its highest level since 2002 — before retreating to close the month near **4.96%** (approx., verify before merging). The initial sell-off was catalyzed by hot inflation data and the FOMC's split 10-2 hold with two explicit dissenters, while the subsequent rally was powered primarily by risk-off safe-haven flows as the AI-driven equity sell-off generated flight-to-quality demand powerful enough to temporarily override the inflationary signal from crude at multi-year highs.

The 2-year Treasury yield settled near **4.63%** (approx., verify before merging) by late October, leaving the 10-year/2-year spread modestly positive at approximately **+33 basis points** (approx., verify before merging) — a mild flattening as short-end yields declined fractionally less than the long end. For duration investors, October's yield retreat from the **5.36%** intraday peak provided meaningful relief; but its sustainability is widely questioned given elevated oil prices and an explicitly hawkish Fed that has telegraphed further tightening. The December FOMC meeting — expected to deliver a **25 basis point** hike — will likely resolve the central tension: if inflation remains elevated and the Fed acts as projected, long-end yields may reassert the higher-for-longer trajectory that October's risk-off bid temporarily suspended.
